author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Gjoa Haven boil water advisory lifted after months-long disruption
content:
Gjoa Haven residents can now drink tap water without boiling it first, after the Department of Health lifted the community’s boil water advisory, which was in place for nearly seven months.

Last Friday, the Government of Nunavut received two consecutive bacteriological samples for Gjoa Haven, said health department spokesperson Charmaine Deogracias in an interview.

Both tested negative for fecal coliform and total coliform — bacteria that can indicate contamination from human or animal waste.

Regional environmental health officer Sharlene Lively reviewed the results, Deogracias said.

The Department of Health then recommended that the advisory be lifted, with final approval coming from Nunavut Chief Public Health Officer Dr. Ekua Agyemang.

The advisory had been in place since Jan. 16, after a break was discovered in a six-kilometre water main that connected Swan Lake to the community’s water treatment plant.

Although the Hamlet of Gjoa Haven completed repairs to restore the water supply on June 17, the advisory remained in place while Nunavut’s Department of Transportation and Infrastructure cleaned and disinfected the water storage tank.

The tank was flushed on July 24, the department said in an emailed update. The delay was due to scheduling qualified tradespeople, it said.

author: Mosha Folger
title: Sanirajak man sentenced to four and a half years for sex crimes
content:
After a series of delays, Simeonie Issigaitok has received a four-and-a-half year sentence in a federal penitentiary for sexually touching children under the age of 16.

Court staff brought the 73-year-old Sanirajak man from into an Iqaluit courtroom Tuesday in a wheelchair. Through an interpreter, he listened expressionless, occasionally nodding his head, as Justice Christian Lyons read his sentence.

“Vulnerability of Inuit children and, in particular Inuit girls, is demonstrated by the persistent and troublingly high per capita rate of child sexual abuse in Nunavut,” Lyons said. “A problem that Mr. Issigaitok has repeatedly and substantially contributed to for decades.”

Issigaitok pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of sexual interference. The first offence occurred in Sanirajak sometime between 1987 and 1989. Issigaitok assaulted a girl in her early teens at her home while her parents were asleep.

The second incident occurred in April 2021. Issigaitok was captured on security video during a community event touching a boy while he was seated with a group of children.

On Tuesday, Lyons said aggravating factors included Issigaitok’s history of convictions for sex crimes dating back to  which dates back to 1988, his 2014 designation as a dangerous offender, and that his victims were Inuit children.

author: Daron Letts
title: City of Iqaluit, Qikiqtani General Hospital team up to fight cancer
content:
A new cancer-fighting partnership between the City of Iqaluit and Qikiqtani General Hospital might be the first such collaboration in the world, says the Ontario doctor behind the research that made the partnership possible.

Dr. Matthew Kwon, a family physician at the hospital, made a pitch to city council July 28 to waive fees at the Iqaluit Aquatic Centre for 10 cancer patients, based on research in an article in the June 2025 edition of the New England Journal of Medicine .

Kwon is working on the project with Dr. Alexandra Borwein, who also works at the hospital.

“Exercise may be as effective in some instances in preventing recurrences of cancer as some of the other treatments that we currently use,” Borwein said Thursday in an interview.

Titled “ Structured Exercise after Adjuvant Chemotherapy for Colon Cancer,” the article outlines a study conducted between 2009 and 2024 at 55 health centres around the world, most of them in Canada and Australia. It was funded by the Canadian Cancer Society.

The randomized clinical trials involved close to 900 colorectal cancer patients, half of whom received free guided athletic training. The other half were given educational materials for self-guided exercise.

The research found patients in the structured exercise program had a 37 per cent lower risk of death and a 28 per cent lower risk of recurrence or developing other cancers.

author: Daron Letts
title: Saved from trash in 1980s, these photos are going home to Kugaaruk
content:
Photographs taken in the 1960s are heading back to one of the Kugaaruk families they depict, thanks to help from an amateur historian based in Nashville.

Lucy Immingark of Kugaaruk plans to display the photos at the hamlet office. (Photo courtesy of Lucy Immingark)

Jim Miller’s late grandmother discovered the photos in the mid-1980s in the trash room of her Burlington, Ont., apartment building. The nine colour images show Inuit building an igloo, drying fish and enjoying the warmth of a qulliq.

Miller said his grandmother knew they meant something to someone, but decades before the internet, finding their origin was not a simple task. The photos ended up mounted to wooden plaques and displayed on the family’s wall before Miller inherited them.

“They’ve been in our house since I was a teenager,” Miller said. “When I moved out, I took them.”

This summer, Miller took the photos out of storage at his home in Peterborough, Ont., and posted them on his wall — and on Reddit. He wanted suggestions for finding them a good home.

“I’ve often wondered if I could find out if the family is still in the community,” Miller said.

Enter Elliott Jakes, an airplane mechanic in Nashville, Tenn.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Documentary brings stories from Inukjuak to international stage
content:
A documentary that celebrates a Nunavik community’s resilience is set to be screened at the International First Peoples Festival in Montreal on Aug. 5.




Directed by Geela Kumarluk and Hannah Walti, 

Inukjuak 

was filmed in spring 2022 but took several years to complete due to a lack of funding. It premièred at the Montreal International Film Festival last August — the same month it was completed.




“We’re really, really happy that it’s at the festival and that it’s gonna be seen,” Walti said in an interview.




She met Kumarluk during a research trip to Inukjuak in December 2021, when Walti was planning to film a documentary.




“She asked me, ‘Is it a true crime?’” Walti said, with a laugh.




Kumarluk, who could not be reached for this story, shared her experiences about life in Inukjuak and described her search to better understand her family’s residential school history, which had remained largely unspoken about, Walti said.




The two decided to explore intergenerational trauma and how the community has tried to overcome it.
















Through interviews with elders, the film depicts the impacts of residential schools, the Nunavik 

dog slaughter

 and the High Arctic 

relocation

, during which the federal government forced Inuit out of communities such as Inukjuak to remote settlements like Grise Fiord and Resolute Bay.

author: Mosha Folger
title: Nunavut sex offender’s sentencing delayed due to poor health
content:
A 72-year-old Sanirajak man set to be sentenced for sex crimes Tuesday in Iqaluit saw his court date delayed due to medical issues.




Simeonie Issigaitok was medevaced to Ottawa earlier this week after experiencing difficulty breathing said defence lawyer Alan Regal in court Tuesday.




“I enquired whether or not he was up for a phone call, and I didn’t have a response from that,” Regel said, relaying information he said he received from staff at Aaqqigiarvik Correctional Healing Facility.




“I’m without instructions, other than to advise the court that he’s not available, and the reason why.”




Issigaitok 

pleaded guilty

 in December 2025 to two counts of sexually touching children under the age of 16, which involved two victims.




The first charge occurred in Sanirajak sometime between 1987 and 1989. The second incident occurred in April 2025.




Crown attorney Jessika Withers agreed that Issigaitok should be present for his sentencing.
















“It’s probably best that we put it off, figure out what’s going on with him,” Withers said Tuesday in court. “With a decision of this magnitude I think it makes sense to have him here, or at least on the phone.”




Justice Christian Lyons accepted the lawyers’ request, and scheduled Issigaitok’s next appearance for Aug. 4.

author: Krista
title: ᐃᓱᖃᕐᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᓄᑖᑦ ᐅᔭᕋᒃᓯᐊᕈᑎᐅᓇᓱᒃᑐᑦ ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᓄᓇᓂ ᐊᑐᕈᑎᒃᓴᖅ ᐊᖏᖅᑕᐅᒃᐸᑦ: ᐃᑲᔪᖃᑦᑕᖅᑐᑦ
content:
For the English version of this story, please see 

Limit new mining claims until land-use plan approved: advocates

.







ᓄᓇᕗᒦᑦᑐᖅ ᓄᓇᒥ ᐊᑐᕈᓐᓇᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᔨᐅᔪᑦ ᐱᖁᔨᔪᑦ ᓄᖅᑲᖅᑎᑦᑎᖁᔨᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᓄᑖᓂ ᐅᔭᕋᒃᓯᐊᕈᑎᐅᔪᓂ ᓴᐳᔾᔨᔭᐅᓯᒪᓇᔭᕐᑐᑦ ᑭᖑᓪᓕᖅᐹᒃᑯᑦ ᑎᑎᕋᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᔪᓂᒃ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᓄᓇᓂ ᐊᑐᕈᑎᒃᓴᓂ ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᓄᑖᓂ ᐸᕐᓇᐅᑎᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓯᐊᓂᒃᐸᑕ.




ᐱᖃᓐᓇᕆᔭᐅᔪᑦ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓄᓇᓂ ᐊᑐᕈᑎᒃᓴᓂ ᐸᕐᓇᐅᑎᓂᒃ ᑐᓂᓯᓚᐅᕐᒪᑕ ᐃᓱᒪᓕᐊᕆᔭᖏᓐᓂ ᔪᓚᐃ 9-ᒥ ᑐᓴᒐᒃᓴᓕᐅᖅᖢᑎᒃ, ᐅᓇ ᓄᓇᓂ ᐊᑐᕈᑎᒃᓴᖅ ᐊᖏᖅᑕᐅᙱᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᑭᖑᓪᓕᖅᐹᒥ.




ᓄᓇᓂ ᐊᑐᕈᑎᒃᓴᓂ ᐸᕐᓇᐅᑎ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᒪᑦ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᓂᖓᓄᑦ 1993-ᒥ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐊᖏᕈᑎᓂ. ᐊᑐᕈᑎᖓ ᐊᕕᒃᓯᒪᑎᑦᑎᓇᓱᒃᖢᓂ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᓇᖕᒥᓂᖅ ᓄᓇᖏᓐᓂ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐊᕙᑎᒋᔭᒧᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐆᒪᔪᐃᑦ ᐃᓂᖏᑦ ᓴᐳᔾᔭᐅᓯᒪᓂᐊᕐᒪᑕ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ.




ᐊᕐᕌᒎᓕᕐᑐᓂᒃ 16-ᓂ, ᑎᓴᒪᓂ ᑎᑎᕋᖅᑕᐅᓂᑯᓂ ᑐᓂᓯᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ – ᑭᓯᐊᓂᓕ ᐊᖏᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᙱᖢᑎᒃ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ – ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᑐᙵᕕᒃᑯᓐᓄᑦ, ᒐᕙᒪᑐᖃᒃᑯᓐᓄᓪᓗ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᓐᓄᑦ. ᑕᒪᕐᒥ ᐱᖓᓱᑦ ᑎᒦᑦ ᐊᑎᓕᐅᕆᐊᖃᕐᒪᑕ ᐸᕐᓇᐅᑎᓂ ᐊᑐᓕᖅᑎᑕᐅᓕᕈᓐᓇᖁᓪᓗᒍ.




ᑭᖑᓪᓕᕐᐹᖅ ᑎᑎᕋᖅᑕᐅᓂᑯ ᐃᓚᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᑐᒃᓯᕋᐅᓯᐊᕐᓂ ᓄᓇᓂ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᕝᕕᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᑐᓂᒃ, ᒪᑐᐃᖓᔪᓂᒃ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᐊᑐᖁᔭᐅᔪᓂ ᐊᑐᕆᐊᖃᖅᖢᑎᒃ, ᐊᒻᒪᓗ “ᐃᓱᖃᕐᓗᑎ ᐊᑐᕐᕕᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᑐᓄᑦ” ᐃᓂᒋᔭᐅᔪᓂ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓕᕆᓂᕐᒥᓪᓗ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᐅᔪᓐᓇᙱᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᒪᑯᓄᖓ ᐊᕙᑎᒋᔭᒧᑦ, ᐃᓕᖅᑯᓯᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐅᕝᕙᓘᓐᓃᑦ ᐃᑦᑕᕐᓂᓴᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ.




ᐊᑎᓕᐅᖅᑎᒋᔭᐅᔪᑦ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᑎᑎᖃᓂ ᔪᓚᐃ 6-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᐃᓱᒪᓕᐅᕆᓯᒪᔪᓂᒃ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᖅᓯᒍᑎᒃᓴᓂᒃ, ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐃᓄᖕᓂ ᐅᖃᖃᑎᖃᕐᓂᕐᓴᐅᖃᑦᑕᖁᔨᓪᓗᑎᒃ.
















ᑕᐃᒪᐃᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ, ᓴᕕᕋᔭᒃᓴᓂ ᕿᓂᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᖅ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᓯᖏᑦᑎᒍᑦ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᓂᖅ ᓱᓕ ᑲᔪᓯᔪᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐸᕐᓇᐅᑎᑕᖃᙱᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




“ᓈᒻᒪᙱᓕᐅᕈᑎᑦ ᓴᖅᑭᑉᐸᓪᓕᐊᓕᕐᑐᑦ. ᒪᐃ 2025-ᒥ, ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᓇᑉᐸᖓᑕ ᐅᖓᑖᓃᑦᑐᑦ ᓄᓇᕗᒥ 52,000 ᑭᑉᐹᕆᒃᓯᒪᔪᓂ ᑭᓛᒥᑕᓂ ᐅᔭᕋᒃᓯᐅᕈᒪᔪᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓯᕕᐅᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐊᕐᕌᒎᓵᖅᑑᖕᓂ ᒪᕐᕉᖕᓂ,” ᐅᖃᕐᓯᒪᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᑐᓴᒐᒃᓴᑦ ᐱᖃᓐᓇᕆᔭᐅᔪᓂᒃ ᓄᓇᓂ ᐊᑐᕈᑎᒃᓴᓄᑦ ᐸᕐᓇᐅᑎᓂ.




ᒫᓂ 15,000 ᑭᑉᐹᕆᒃᓯᒪᔪᓂ ᑭᓛᒥᑕᓂ ᐱᓇᓱᒍᑎᓂ ᒪᑯᓇᓃᑦᑐᑦ ᐃᓱᖃᕐᓗᑎ ᐊᑐᕐᕕᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᑐᓄᑦ ᐃᓂᒋᔭᐅᔪᓂᒃ, ᑕᒫᓂᓗ ᖃᓄᐃ

author: Corey Larocque
title: Buy Canadian? Bring it on
content:
What’s good for Canada is often good for Nunavut and Nunavik. So, as the federal government pushes its Buy Canadian policy to use Canadian-made materials in the construction of new public works projects, it creates a new opportunity for the North.




Federal Public Works and Procurement Minister Joël Lightbound 

announced

 Tuesday the government had picked Inuit-owned Arctic Fresh Projects Inc. to build a $35.6-million, 23-unit apartment building in Iqaluit. It will provide housing for some of the approximately 200 federal government employees in the city.




It’s also one of the first government contracts awarded under the new Buy Canadian policy, a government news release said. Its construction will use predominantly Canadian steel, aluminum, and lumber.




“We’ve been very focused on what we can do to shore up the Canadian economy,” Lightbound said.




Talk about good timing. The news came the day after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a whopping 50-per-cent tariff on a host of Canadian products — including hockey sticks, of all things —beginning in mid-August.




The Buy Canadian policy came into effect in December, spelling out rules to prioritize Canadian suppliers and Canadian-made materials when the government builds new projects. One of the policy’s goals is to help Canadian industries respond to a decline in their traditional U.S. markets.

 Caribou are like lemmings. When one starts crossing, the others follow. But there is no indicator as to when the migration starts.

 There is a “trigger” moment as the ice forms, indicating that caribou instinctively know when it’s safe to cross.




C.

 There is no rhyme or reason to the crossing. They go when they feel like it.
